name: Balangao
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_citation: Shetler, Joanne. 1976. Notes on Balangao Grammar. Language Data, Asian-Pacific Series 9. Huntington Beach, CA: Summer Institute of Linguistics. (full PDF, 257 pp., SIL archive entry 4048 via the Internet Archive)
catalog_quote: Word stress in Balangao is phonemic, occurring on the ultimate or penultimate syllable of a full grammatical word, with or without affixes. All full words (see Sec. 1.1) must have stress. 'hawang 'doorway', ha'wang 'reach inside with hands', 'qale 'come', qa'le 'word'. A secondary stress occurs on every second syllable counting back from the main stress: pa"gingi'nahal 'sandy place', "bale'ngawngaw 'circle', qo"menpa"bale'ngawngaw 'cause it to be circled'. Clitics also have stress and they are the only full grammatical words that may occur as a single syllable with a single mora of length. ... Clitics do not set up secondary stress. ... Stress is characterized by 1) an added mora of vowel length when it occurs on non-final CV syllables, 2) a slight rise in pitch, and 3) intensity ...
sweep_summary: Balangao (bala1310) is in the catalog as 'lexical' on Shetler 1976 (Notes on Balangao Grammar, Sec. 1.5 p. 31: stress phonemic, ultimate or penultimate). this search of works with stress in the title found one stress-titled item, Shetler & Fetzer 1964 'The Obscuring of Word Accent in Balangao' (Oceanic Linguistics 3(1):101-109, DOI 10.2307/3622942), already in our bibliography; it is plainly about word accent in this language (Glottolog subject 'Suprasegmentals'; Shetler 1966 n. 4 names it as the detailed treatment). No open copy exists: Semantic Scholar and Unpaywall report it closed, JSTOR is paywalled behind a JS challenge, the archive.org microfilm scan of OL 3(1) is lending-restricted (text and search-inside blocked), HathiTrust has OL search-only and lacks vol. 3, Google Books and SIL entry 12319 return nothing. It is marked not-read, priority medium (same author as the 1976 grammar, so expected to corroborate, not change, the classification). The only first-hand statement read this search of works with stress in the title is Shetler 1966 'Balangao Phonemes' (PL A-8, open: 'Word accent is also a phonemic feature of the dialect' (p. 2) and 'Accent is contrastive on the word level' (p. 7), with all accented examples on the final two syllables; it confirms but does not supersede the catalog source.

new_statements.quote: Words may be full words or semi words. Semi words carry no stress and have only one mora of vowel length, i.e. one vowel. This is the case with single particles and certain adjuncts, so they are classed as semi words. Full words carry stress and have at least two moras of vowel length. Most commonly these two moras of length are realized by two syllables. However, a few words occur with two historical vowels fused into one long vowel with two moras of length. Stress always occurs on these fused vowels, resisting the normal morphophonemic change of stress upon suffixation (see Sec. 1.61).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Every full (bimoraic) word carries one stress; monomoraic particles/adjuncts ('semi words') are unstressed. No placement rule is given in the excerpted pages, but every marked example falls on the final or penultimate syllable ('qaho 'dog' vs lu'wang 'carabao'; 'pakpak vs pa'pa; 'kalo vs qa'lo; ka'bayyu, pos'laqet, dip'lat), i.e. lexically placed within the last two syllables; stress normally shifts under suffixation (Sec. 1.61 'Stress Shift', e.g. lan'sa + -en = lan'seen 'nail it'), except that fused long vowels (buuq 'hair', miid 'there is none') always keep the stress. The dedicated Stress section (1.5) and Stress Shift section (1.61) exist in the full book but are outside the open excerpt; the full SIL PDF is could not be reached by automated download (not reachable by automated download twice) and the Internet Archive copy host is could not be reached by automated download.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the excerpted pages (ToC has '1.51 Stress Group' and '1.52 Intonation Group', not seen).
new_statements.exceptions: Fused long vowels always carry stress and resist the normal stress shift upon suffixation; semi words (single particles, certain adjuncts) carry no stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Shetler 1976 (Introduction, pp. 16-17, file rosettaproject_blw_detail-1) describes Balangao of Natonin Municipality, Mt. Province, and notes two sub-dialects, Balangao proper (Balangao, Botac, Santa Isabel, Banawel) and Hagi (Tonglayan, Alnugan), differing only in central-vowel allophony and palatalization of b; the phonology is written for Balangao proper. The listed Reid 1971 open item describes Ilongot (Kakiduge:n Bugkalut, ISO ilk), a different language.

tone_statements.quote: 2. Both word accent and intonation involve three details: (1) long vs short vowels (LENGTH), (2) pitch or high vs low tones (PITCH ACCENT), (3) loudness or amplitude (STRESS). [...] (Examples could also be drawn from Butuanon, Cebuano, Balangaw, Bontok, Hanunoo, Ibanag, Isneg, Kamayo, Sambal, etc.) [...] 3. sources.note: States that Philippine word accent (contrastive in many but not all Philippine languages, Balangaw listed among the examples) involves length, pitch accent ('high vs low tones') and stress, ranks length as the primary phonemic feature and pitch above loudness as the audible cue, and holds that stress or pitch accent is a phrase-level (syntactic) feature that need not coincide with length and can be overridden by intonation. sources.note: Classifies Balangaw under (A) 'Phonemic length and shortness, as inherited from PPH', i.e. an inherited contrastive-accent (quantity) language, and names it among languages illustrating 'the interplay of length, pitch and stress in contrastive word accent'; argues generally that pitch, not loudness, is the salient cue and that vowel length is the primary feature of Philippine word accent. Nothing specific to Balangao beyond the classification; no lexical tone claimed.
